Well, I came back from my trip to Japan and I think it was a good experience, albeit not ideal. The things I adore/miss the most would be the convenience stores and train systems (the jingles and all)since I spent most of my time there, but it was definitely a culture shock, even for me, particularly Akiba. I initially went in to giggle and joke around, but when I saw the pachinko parlors and people buying up all that hentai like buying groceries in a convenience store, I was just devastated. Sensory overload would probably be one way of describing it. To the extent where I fell down a flight of stairs because my legs went limp. All in all, it was good and I would like to return again in the future, but I would certainly not want to live there long-term. The lack of dryers and older buildings smelling like mold all the time is too much of a drawback for me.

Anyways, what I really wanted to post here was basically the story I started writing prior to going to Japan. I had done some research in the past related to hikikomoris, shut-ins, internet cafes, and sentiments of a desolate life in all the glitz and glamour. It was definitely one experience of writing everything out and I was kind of impressed of what I wrote was so strikingly accurate to reality. But even if it was accurate, experiencing it in person was definitely different than writing it out. It felt similar, but had different vibes.

I got bored on the last few days of the trip (I went for 14 days) so rather than exploring Japan for "vacation", I started going around the more seedy places for an adrenaline rush, or rather, material to supplement my story. I went to a few internet cafes, but without a booking or spending money for their service, the attendants never let me in. Initially, I planned on staying for one night, but the cigarette smoke was way too much for me. It was mild relative to the pachinko parlors, but I still couldn't tolerate it. I ended up staying in a new capsule hotel a redditor recommended to me for the last 2 nights I was there.

But I digress, when I was in Shinjuku, I was really curious. I was walking the streets of Shinjuku (passively -- not realizing this was the setting I initially laid out in my story) and saw a girl (I thought she was borderline homeless given her attire) enter a building. The exterior reminded me of the Hong Kong apartments when I went to when I was a kid so I suppose there was some degree of nostalgia attached to this. Anyways, I tailed her and at the same time, I recognized it. Manboo. The same chain of internet cafes that I remember looking into when I was researching and thought this was a perfect opportunity to see if I could get in. But of course, I couldn't walk too far beyond the eyes of the attendant. However, those 30 seconds probably gave me enough reason not to go any further. The atmosphere was dismally inundated with cigarette smoke and raucous with chatter.

I got bored from working on trivial programming exercises today and wanted to write again. I was trying to find Youtube videos because I know there must be a whole cache of videos available online of foreigners cataloging their experiences online and eventually stumbled upon this:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MtdupS0gRt0

What really struck me to the core was how there were people who lived in these places on a permanent basis, similar to a character I created or envisioned I suppose, in the second chapter. A lot of the times when I was in Japan, I couldn't help but feel sorry for a lot of the hard working people there who inevitably get tangled in the web of capitalism we live in today. 700 yen/hour for a cashier? Talk about brutal. The empty malls and workers in Omotesando Hills? Talk about sad. I even recorded about a minute of some French guy trying to cut a deal with some Japanese girl (who either worked or presumably owned some kind of high-end fedora selling store) which inevitably reminded me of China Blue (a documentary about how these Chinese workers got paid about an $1/month). I mean it's not extreme to that extent, but I couldn't help but harbor those same feelings again.

The trip was somewhat tantamount to an epiphany or eye opener in the sense that it made me appreciate more of the things I had in America, but in some sense, it also left me high and dry since the food there is much more remarkable than what we mostly have in the states.
